> A courtroom framing of the design decision behind `visstat()`'s
> central-tendency routing. Not vignette prose — a rhetorical summary that
> states the position and cuts down each counter-argument in turn. Citation
> keys match `vignettes/REFERENCES.bib` (`@Harrell-BBR` is a placeholder).

## The charge

The prosecution imagines a package boasting that it finds the *right* test.
My client makes no such boast. Faced with a numeric response and groups, it
does one modest thing: it chooses a **test of central tendency** --- mean-based
or rank-based --- and prints, on every plot, which one it chose. Transparency,
not optimality. The whole case turns on that distinction.

## The counts, answered

- **"Pre-testing for normality is forbidden" [@Franc:2025].** The objection is
  to *conditional* error in a single arm; my client is judged as a *whole
  procedure*, where the level stays nominal across distributions from skew 0 to
  6 [@Rochon:2012], confirmed in its own simulations. The worst that can be said
  is that pre-testing is *unnecessary* --- not that it inflates error.

- **"The 50-versus-100 threshold is arbitrary."** It was. So my client removed
  it. Sample size never governed the real question; *shape* does. There is now
  no threshold to attack.

- **"Shapiro--Wilk is a normality test, not a skewness test."** It is an omnibus
  statistic, built from neither moment, yet its power is dominated by skewness
  [@DAgostino:1973; @Razali:2011] --- the feature that decides whether a mean
  still describes the data. A proxy, yes: the *honest* one, the diagnostic
  already on the analyst's screen.

- **"At large N it over-rejects and sends mild skew to the rank test."** It does.
  The cost is *not* power --- rank tests keep ~95% efficiency under normality and
  gain under skew [@Bridge:1999; @Harrell-BBR]. The only change is the question
  asked, from means to ordering --- and my client *announces* it.

- **"At small N it misses skew and stays parametric."** Only at sizes so small
  (five, ten per group) that no test can save the analysis. One cannot convict
  my client for failing where statistics itself has already failed.

- **"Then just always use Welch" [@Delacre:2019].** Valid --- but it fixes the
  question to *the mean*, in silence, even for income-type data where the mean
  misleads.

- **"Then always use ranks" [@Harrell-BBR].** Except the rank test answers
  $P(X>Y)=0.5$, which under unequal variances differs from both the means and the
  medians [@Fagerland:2009]: it cries "difference" when the centres are identical.

  Both prosecutions demand my client commit, a priori and unannounced, to a
  single question. Its only offence is refusing to hide that choice.

- **"Why keep the mean branch at all?"** Because under normality those tests are
  uniformly most powerful, and they alone return an effect and a confidence
  interval on the data's own scale [@Bridge:1999; @Harrell-BBR]. The rank branch
  buys robustness; the mean branch buys interpretability. My client discards
  neither --- it routes, and it reports.

## Closing

My client cannot know your research question; no automated tool can. So it does
the only honest thing available: it reads the shape of the data, makes a
transparent, overridable choice between comparing means and comparing ranks, and
shows every diagnostic behind that choice.

It never claimed to be optimal. It claimed to be *legible*. On the only charge
that was ever real --- concealment --- my client is innocent, because concealment
is the one thing it was built never to do.

The defence rests.
